title: Republic Book II: Socrates on justice as a good in itself, the city in speech, and the guardians' nature
summary: Glaucon and Adeimantus ask Socrates to praise justice for its effect on the soul alone, without reputation or reward. Socrates ranks justice among goods wanted for themselves and for their results, then builds a city in speech to see justice at large. He ends by shaping the guardians' philosophic nature and by rejecting false stories about the gods.

principles.text: Justice belongs with the highest goods: wanted both for its own sake and for its results.
principles.quote: In the highest class, I replied, --among those goods which he who would be happy desires both for their own sake and for the sake of their results.

principles.text: To find justice in the soul, look first at the city, where it is larger and easier to see.
principles.quote: Then in the larger the quantity of justice is likely to be larger and more easily discernible.

principles.text: A city arises from need: no one is self-sufficient, so people gather helpers and exchange for mutual good.
principles.quote: A State, I said, arises, as I conceive, out of the needs of mankind; no one is self-sufficing, but all of us have many wants.

principles.text: Work is best done when each person does the one thing suited to their nature, at the right time.
principles.quote: all things are produced more plentifully and easily and of a better quality when one man does one thing which is natural to him and does it at the right time, and leaves other things.

principles.text: Philosophy is love of learning: telling friend from stranger by knowing and not knowing marks the philosophic nature.
principles.quote: Why, because he distinguishes the face of a friend and of an enemy only by the criterion of knowing and not knowing.

principles.text: The worst lie is ignorance in the soul about the highest realities, and everyone hates to hold it there.
principles.quote: deception, or being deceived or uninformed about the highest realities in the highest part of themselves, which is the soul, and in that part of them to have and to hold the lie, is what mankind least like
